stem: A 55-year-old man has had blood pressure readings of 152/96 mm Hg at three visits despite taking metoprolol. His serum calcium is 9.4 mg/dL and his creatinine is normal. Hydrochlorothiazide is added.
oneliner: 55M + BP 152/96 on 3 visits despite metoprolol + normal calcium and creatinine + hydrochlorothiazide added → how does it work?
ask: The added drug lowers his blood pressure initially by acting at which of the following sites?

options.A: Inhibiting the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb
options.B: Inhibiting the Na-Cl symporter in the distal convoluted tubule
options.C: Blocking aldosterone receptors in the collecting duct
options.D: Blocking epithelial sodium channels in the collecting duct
options.E: Inhibiting carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule

whyNot.A: **Loop diuretics** (furosemide): a different drug and a different segment
whyNot.C: **Spironolactone / eplerenone** act here; thiazides do not
whyNot.D: **Amiloride / triamterene** act here; thiazides do not

answer: Na-Cl symporter block in the distal convoluted tubule (thiazide)
why: **Hydrochlorothiazide** is a thiazide. It **blocks the Na-Cl symporter in the distal convoluted tubule**, so more sodium and water are excreted and volume and pressure fall.

drug.name: Hydrochlorothiazide
drug.how: Blocks the Na-Cl symporter in the distal convoluted tubule
drug.use: Hypertension, edema, nephrolithiasis (calcium), nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
drug.watch: Hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypercalcemia, hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia, hyperlipidemia; sulfa allergy

stem: A 66-year-old woman with heart failure still has pitting leg edema on furosemide. Her serum potassium has fallen from 4.2 to 3.0 mEq/L, and her creatinine is normal. Amiloride is added to her regimen.
oneliner: 66F + heart failure + edema persists on furosemide + K 4.2 → 3.0 + amiloride added → how does it raise potassium?
ask: Amiloride corrects her potassium mainly through which of the following?

options.A: Blocking aldosterone receptors in the collecting duct
options.B: Blocking luminal sodium channels in the collecting duct
options.C: Stimulating the Na-K ATPase in principal cells
options.D: Inhibiting the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb
options.E: Increasing sodium delivery to the distal nephron

whyNot.A: **Spironolactone / eplerenone**: a different drug; amiloride does not need aldosterone
whyNot.C: **Increases** potassium secretion; no diuretic does this
whyNot.E: **Loop and thiazide effect**: this is what lowered her potassium

answer: ENaC block in the collecting duct (amiloride, triamterene)
why: **Amiloride and triamterene block ENaC** in the collecting duct. Less sodium enters the principal cell, the lumen is **less negative**, so **less potassium is secreted** and potassium stays in the body.

drug.name: Amiloride / triamterene
drug.how: Blocks epithelial sodium channels in the collecting duct, so less K+ is secreted
drug.use: Adding to loop or thiazide to prevent hypokalemia; amiloride for lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
drug.watch: Hyperkalemia (especially with ACE inhibitors or kidney disease); triamterene can cause kidney stones

chain: Less sodium enters, lumen less negative

stem: A 61-year-old man with hypertension takes part in a trial of a new diuretic. After 3 days his weight is down 2 kg and his standing blood pressure has fallen. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.50 and bicarbonate 34 mEq/L; serum potassium is 3.1 mEq/L and urinary calcium excretion has increased.
oneliner: 61M + new diuretic trial + 3 d later weight down 2 kg + pH 7.50, HCO3 34, K 3.1 + urine calcium up → drug works how?
ask: The new drug most likely acts by which of the following mechanisms?

options.A: Inhibiting the Na-Cl symporter in the distal convoluted tubule
options.B: Inhibiting carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
options.C: Blocking epithelial sodium channels in the collecting duct
options.D: Blocking aldosterone receptors in the collecting duct
options.E: Inhibiting the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb

whyNot.A: **Thiazides**: also cause alkalosis, but they **lower** urinary calcium
whyNot.C: **K-sparing**: potassium would be high or normal, not low
whyNot.D: **K-sparing**: potassium would be high or normal, not low

answer: NKCC2 block in the thick ascending limb (loop diuretic)
why: **Volume loss + metabolic alkalosis + low potassium + more urine calcium** = a loop diuretic. It **blocks NKCC2** in the thick ascending limb, which also removes the positive lumen voltage that drives calcium reabsorption.

drug.name: Furosemide (loop diuretics)
drug.how: Blocks the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb
drug.use: Edema (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome), hypercalcemia, acute pulmonary edema
drug.watch: Ototoxicity, hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, dehydration; sulfa allergy (not ethacrynic acid)

chain: Volume contraction, K+ and H+ lost

stem: A 69-year-old man with bilateral renal artery stenosis has a stable creatinine of 1.4 mg/dL. After 5 days of ibuprofen for knee pain, his creatinine is 2.6 mg/dL. Urinalysis is bland, with no white cell casts, no eosinophils and no rash.
oneliner: 69M + bilateral renal artery stenosis + Cr 1.4 → 2.6 after 5 d of ibuprofen + bland urine, no eosinophils, no rash → how did the drug raise creatinine?
ask: The rise in creatinine is best explained by which drug effect?

options.A: Loss of angiotensin II constriction of the efferent arteriole
options.B: Loss of prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriole dilation
options.C: Allergic inflammation of the renal interstitium
options.D: Immune complex deposition in the glomeruli
options.E: Direct toxicity to the proximal tubule epithelium

whyNot.A: Occurs with **ACE inhibitors**, and he is not taking one
whyNot.C: Would give **rash, fever, eosinophils**; none here
whyNot.D: Would give **active sediment with red cell casts**; urine is bland
whyNot.E: Would give **muddy brown casts**; urine is bland

answer: Less prostaglandin, afferent arteriole constricts, GFR falls (NSAID)
why: In **renal artery stenosis** GFR depends on **prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilation**. **NSAIDs block cyclooxygenase**, the afferent arteriole constricts, and GFR falls with a bland sediment.

drug.name: Ibuprofen (NSAIDs)
drug.how: Reversibly blocks COX-1 and COX-2, lowering prostaglandin synthesis
drug.use: Pain, inflammation, fever, patent ductus arteriosus closure (indomethacin)
drug.watch: Gastric ulcers, AKI (afferent constriction), interstitial nephritis, analgesic nephropathy, fluid retention, hypertension

stem: A 52-year-old woman has had a sudden urge to urinate and has been passing small volumes about every 90 minutes for 6 months. She has no pain or burning, and urinalysis and post-void residual volume are normal. Oxybutynin is prescribed.
oneliner: 52F + 6 mo urgency, frequent small voids + no dysuria + normal urinalysis and residual volume + oxybutynin prescribed → how does it work?
ask: Oxybutynin relieves her symptoms mainly through which of the following?

options.A: Blocking alpha-1 receptors at the bladder neck
options.B: Blocking nicotinic receptors at autonomic ganglia
options.C: Blocking muscarinic receptors on the detrusor muscle
options.D: Stimulating muscarinic receptors on the detrusor muscle

whyNot.A: **Tamsulosin**: used for outflow obstruction in men with BPH
whyNot.B: **Ganglionic blockers**: not used for the bladder; broad side effects
whyNot.D: **Bethanechol**: would worsen urgency; used for retention
whyNot.E: **Finasteride**: shrinks the prostate; she has none

why: **Urgency and frequency without infection or retention** = overactive bladder. **Oxybutynin is an antimuscarinic**: it blocks M3 receptors on the detrusor, so the bladder relaxes and urgency falls.

drug.name: Oxybutynin
drug.how: Blocks M3 muscarinic receptors on the detrusor muscle
drug.watch: Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention, confusion in older adults

stem: A 67-year-old man has hesitancy, a weak stream and nocturia three times a night for a year. Rectal examination shows a smooth, symmetrically enlarged prostate, and PSA is 2.1 ng/mL. Tamsulosin is started and his stream improves within a few days.
oneliner: 67M + hesitancy, weak stream, nocturia x3 + smooth enlarged prostate + PSA 2.1 + tamsulosin started, better within days → how does it work?
ask: The rapid improvement is best explained by which of the following?

options.B: Blocking muscarinic receptors on the detrusor
options.C: Blocking alpha-1 receptors in prostate smooth muscle
options.D: Stimulating muscarinic receptors on the detrusor

whyNot.A: **Finasteride**: shrinks the gland over **months**, not days
whyNot.B: **Oxybutynin**: could worsen retention in an obstructed bladder
whyNot.D: **Bethanechol**: used for retention from a weak detrusor
whyNot.E: **Neostigmine**: used for retention without obstruction; not for BPH

answer: Alpha-1 blockade relaxes prostate smooth muscle
why: **Smooth enlarged prostate + obstructive symptoms** = BPH. **Tamsulosin blocks alpha-1A receptors**, the prostate and bladder-neck smooth muscle relaxes, urethral resistance falls, and flow improves within days.

drug.name: Tamsulosin (also terazosin, doxazosin)
drug.how: Blocks alpha-1 receptors in prostate and bladder neck smooth muscle
drug.watch: Orthostatic hypotension, dizziness, retrograde ejaculation, floppy iris syndrome in cataract surgery
